issues.legal_issue: A Collector’s decision determining possession or rent after a dispute over an allegedly invalid alienation of hereditary-office land is quasi-judicial when the governing scheme requires an inquiry and the decision affects the parties’ property rights.
material_facts: The dispute concerned hereditary-office land held by one branch of a family and claimed by the officiator from another branch.
The Collector’s statutory process required a reasoned determination concerning the alienation and empowered the Collector to evict a person in wrongful possession or require rent.
The decision affected the parties’ rights to the land and could be challenged by appeal or revision.
The inquiry involved the competing parties and consideration of evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Collector’s decision was quasi-judicial, not administrative; the statutory process, including the consequential decision about possession or rent, was quasi-judicial in character.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 11 and 12 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, read with the statutory appeal and revision scheme in sections 77 and 79, a decision resolving a dispute over land after an inquiry and affecting rights is quasi-judicial. The existence of discretion over the form of relief does not make the decision administrative, and general administrative control under section 74 does not alter that character. The Court relied on Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. Andhra Pradesh Road Transport Corporation and Board of High School and Intermediate Education, U.P. v. Ghanshyam Das Gupta; it distinguished Robinson v. Minister of Town and Country Planning and Franklin v. Minister of Town and Country Planning because the statutory schemes and nature of the disputes differed.

rule.if: land_possession_dispute and reasoned_inquiry_required and decision_affects_property_rights and decision_subject_to_appeal_or_revision

predicates.land_possession_dispute: A proceeding concerns competing claims to possession of land.
predicates.reasoned_inquiry_required: The governing process requires an inquiry and a reasoned determination before the decision is made.
predicates.decision_affects_property_rights: The decision determines or affects the parties’ rights concerning the property.
predicates.decision_subject_to_appeal_or_revision: The decision may be challenged through an appeal or revision provided by the governing scheme.

issues.definition: When a land-possession dispute is decided after a required reasoned inquiry, the decision affects property rights, and the decision is subject to appeal or revision, the Collector’s decision is quasi-judicial.

issues.legal_issue: The Government cannot review or modify its final quasi-judicial order made in revision unless the governing law expressly confers a power of review.
material_facts: The Government investigated the competing claims, gave the parties an opportunity to present evidence, and made an order restoring the land to the applicant.
The order was made in the exercise of revisional authority, although it did not expressly cite the relevant statutory provisions.
On a later application by the occupants, the Government altered its earlier order to allow them to retain possession on payment of rent.
The governing law contained no express provision authorizing the Government to review its revisional order.
issues.conclusion: The Government’s later modification was ultra vires and beyond its jurisdiction because the earlier revisional order was quasi-judicial and final, and there was no express power to review it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 79 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, empowered the relevant authorities to make or revise the land-related order, but did not confer a power on the Government to review its own final revisional order. A revisional authority acts judicially or quasi-judicially, and its order cannot be altered as though it were an administrative order subject to general control under section 74. The Court relied on the quasi-judicial principles in Gullapalli Nageswara Rao and Board of High School and Intermediate Education, U.P. v. Ghanshyam Das Gupta.

predicates.review_of_revisional_adjudication: The proceeding concerns a later attempt by an authority to reconsider an order it previously made in revision.
predicates.prior_order_resolved_contested_rights: The earlier order resolved competing claims after an inquiry and determined rights affecting the parties.
predicates.no_express_review_power: The governing law does not expressly authorize the authority to review its own revisional order.

issues.definition: If an authority later reconsiders its revisional adjudication of contested rights without an express review power, its later review order is without jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A delay in seeking revision does not by itself prevent the Government from exercising revisional authority when the governing law prescribes no limitation period; the Government determines whether the delay is reasonable.
material_facts: The Government’s revisional order followed an application concerning an order made many years earlier.
The governing Act specified no period of limitation for an application for revision.
The Government considered that there were strong reasons to interfere despite the lapse of time.
issues.conclusion: The age of the earlier order did not prevent the Government’s action from being treated as an exercise of quasi-judicial revisional power; the Government determines what is a reasonable time in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, specified no limitation period for an application for revision. In the absence of such a period, the Government would normally act only if moved within a reasonable time, and what is reasonable in a particular case is for the Government to consider.

predicates.revision_proceeding: The matter is an application asking the Government to exercise revisional authority over an earlier order.
predicates.no_statutory_revision_deadline: The governing law sets no limitation period for seeking revision.
predicates.government_considers_delay_reasonable: The Government considers the circumstances and finds a sufficient basis to act despite the delay.

issues.definition: When a revision proceeding has no statutory deadline and the Government considers the delay reasonable in the circumstances, the Government may consider the delayed revision.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar on civil suits concerning hereditary-office property does not prevent a civil court from hearing a suit in which the Government is only a formal party and the substantive relief is against private occupants, including where the court must determine whether a limited tribunal exceeded its authority.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought possession and related relief against the private occupants of the land.
The Government was joined, but it did not possess the land or actively obstruct recovery of possession; the court treated it as a formal party.
The challenged later orders were alleged to be beyond the Government’s jurisdiction and void.
The suit did not require substantive relief against the Government.
issues.conclusion: The statutory exclusion did not bar the suit because no relief was in fact sought against the Government; the civil court could determine whether the authority had exceeded its statutory powers.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(a) of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, bars specified claims against the Government relating to hereditary-office property, but did not apply where the Government was merely a formal party and no substantive relief was sought against it. Civil courts retain jurisdiction to determine whether a tribunal of limited jurisdiction acted within its statutory powers. The Court relied on Ramrao Jankiram Kadam v. State of Bombay, Province of Bombay v. Hormusji Manekji, and The Secretary of State v. Musk & Co.; it distinguished Shrimant Sardan Bhujangarao Daulatrao Ghorpade v. Shrimant Malojirao Daulatrao Ghorpade on the basis that the claim there could not be separated from the relief sought against the Government.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_limited_authority: A civil suit asks the court to determine whether a tribunal or authority acted within the powers granted to it.
predicates.government_is_only_formal_party: The Government is joined in the suit but no substantive relief is sought against it.
predicates.substantive_relief_targets_private_occup: The substantive relief sought is directed against private persons possessing or obstructing access to the property.

issues.definition: If a civil suit challenges the limits of an authority’s power, the Government is only a formal party, and substantive relief is sought against private occupants, the civil court may hear the suit.
